blocks.content: Single Sign-On, or SSO, lets a user log in once and then access many separate applications without logging in again. Sign in to your company account in the morning, and email, chat, the wiki, and the deployment dashboard all just let you in.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277772200-336502459.png

Behind that smooth experience sits a shared identity provider that every application trusts. This page explains what SSO is, the roles involved, how a login actually flows across applications, the protocols that make it work, and how to discuss it in a system design interview.
1. The Problem SSO Solves
A modern company or product often runs dozens of applications. Without SSO, each one keeps its own username and password. This creates real pain for both users and the organization.

["Users juggle many passwords, so they reuse weak ones or write them down.","Every application must build and secure its own login, password reset, and account storage.","When someone leaves, an admin has to disable them in every system separately, and one missed account is a security hole.","There is no single place to enforce policies such as multi factor authentication."]
items: Users juggle many passwords, so they reuse weak ones or write them down.
Every application must build and secure its own login, password reset, and account storage.
When someone leaves, an admin has to disable them in every system separately, and one missed account is a security hole.
There is no single place to enforce policies such as multi factor authentication.

blocks.content: SSO fixes this by moving authentication into one trusted service. Applications stop storing passwords and instead ask that service who the user is.

blocks.title: The one line summary
blocks.content: SSO means one login, checked by one trusted identity provider, unlocks many applications that all trust it.
2. The Core Idea: One Identity Provider
blocks.text: 2. The Core Idea: One Identity Provider

blocks.content: The heart of SSO is a single identity provider that owns authentication. Every application delegates the "who is this user" question to it, instead of answering that question itself.

Because there is one place where login happens, there is one place to enforce strong passwords, one place to require multi factor authentication, and one place to instantly cut off access. Applications only need to trust the identity provider and read the proof it hands out.
Centralize authentication, distribute trust. Applications never see the password; they only trust the token the identity provider issues.
3. Identity Provider vs Service Provider
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277774133-803037767.png
blocks.alt: Identity provider serves many service providers

blocks.content: SSO discussions use two role names constantly, so it helps to fix them early.

["Identity Provider (IdP): the service that authenticates the user and vouches for their identity, such as Okta, Azure AD, or Google Workspace.","Service Provider (SP): any application the user wants to use, such as the wiki or the dashboard. It relies on the IdP and is sometimes called the relying party."]
items: Identity Provider (IdP): the service that authenticates the user and vouches for their identity, such as Okta, Azure AD, or Google Workspace.
Service Provider (SP): any application the user wants to use, such as the wiki or the dashboard. It relies on the IdP and is sometimes called the relying party.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Role","Responsibility","Examples"],"rows":[["Identity Provider","Verifies the user and issues proof of identity","Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace"],["Service Provider","Trusts the IdP and grants access based on that proof","Internal wiki, chat, dashboards"]]}
One identity provider typically serves many service providers. That fan out is exactly what makes a single login unlock many applications.
4. How an SSO Login Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277775772-9405089.png
blocks.alt: First app logs in, later apps are seamless

blocks.content: The first login of the day and every login after it feel different, because of a session held at the identity provider. Here is the first time a user visits an application.

["The user opens Application A and is not yet signed in.","Application A redirects the user to the identity provider.","The identity provider authenticates the user, for example with a password and a second factor.","The identity provider creates its own session and sends the user back to Application A with a signed proof of identity.","Application A validates that proof, creates its own local session, and lets the user in."]
items: The user opens Application A and is not yet signed in.
Application A redirects the user to the identity provider.
The identity provider authenticates the user, for example with a password and a second factor.
The identity provider creates its own session and sends the user back to Application A with a signed proof of identity.
Application A validates that proof, creates its own local session, and lets the user in.

blocks.content: Now the user opens Application B. Application B also redirects to the identity provider, but this time the identity provider already has an active session for this user, so it skips the login screen and immediately returns fresh proof. To the user, Application B simply opened with no login at all.

blocks.title: Where the magic lives
blocks.content: The seamless second login is not magic in the applications. It is the identity provider recognizing its own existing session and issuing new proof without asking for credentials again.
5. A Concrete Walkthrough
Picture an employee starting their day. Their company uses one identity provider for every internal tool.

["They open the email app, which sees no session and redirects them to the company identity provider.","They enter their password and approve a push notification on their phone as a second factor.","The identity provider creates a central session and sends them back to email, signed in.","An hour later they open the deployment dashboard, which also redirects to the identity provider.","The identity provider sees its active session, skips all prompts, and the dashboard opens instantly."]
items: They open the email app, which sees no session and redirects them to the company identity provider.
They enter their password and approve a push notification on their phone as a second factor.
The identity provider creates a central session and sends them back to email, signed in.
An hour later they open the deployment dashboard, which also redirects to the identity provider.
The identity provider sees its active session, skips all prompts, and the dashboard opens instantly.

blocks.content: One password entry and one second factor in the morning unlocked every tool for the rest of the day. When the employee leaves the company, disabling their single identity provider account cuts off all of those tools at once.
6. SSO Protocols Overview
SSO is a pattern, not a single technology. Several protocols implement it, and interviews often ask you to compare them.

{"headers":["Protocol","Style","Best fit"],"rows":[["SAML 2.0","XML assertions, browser redirects","Enterprise and corporate applications"],["OpenID Connect","JSON and JWT on top of OAuth 2.0","Modern web and mobile apps"],["OAuth 2.0","Authorization framework, identity added by OIDC","Delegated API access, basis for OIDC"]]}

SAML is the long standing enterprise choice and speaks XML. OpenID Connect is the modern choice, uses JSON and JWTs, and is friendlier to mobile and single page applications. OAuth by itself handles access, and OpenID Connect is the identity layer built over it.
7. SAML Based SSO
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277777642-962232497.png

SAML, the Security Assertion Markup Language, has powered enterprise SSO for years. Its core artifact is a signed XML document called an assertion, which states who the user is and what attributes they have.

["The service provider generates an authentication request and redirects the browser to the identity provider.","The identity provider authenticates the user and builds a signed SAML assertion.","The browser posts that assertion back to the service provider.","The service provider verifies the signature against the identity provider certificate and logs the user in."]
items: The service provider generates an authentication request and redirects the browser to the identity provider.
The identity provider authenticates the user and builds a signed SAML assertion.
The browser posts that assertion back to the service provider.
The service provider verifies the signature against the identity provider certificate and logs the user in.

blocks.content: The signature is what makes the assertion trustworthy. The service provider does not talk to the identity provider directly for each login; it simply verifies the signature using a certificate exchanged ahead of time.
Why enterprises still use it

SAML predates modern token formats, and countless corporate applications already speak it. It is battle tested, supports rich user attributes, and integrates with established directory systems. Its weaknesses are verbosity and the awkwardness of handling XML in browsers and mobile apps, which is exactly where OIDC shines.
8. OIDC Based SSO
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396521157-720587433.png
blocks.alt: OIDC issues a signed ID token as a JWT

blocks.content: OpenID Connect achieves the same outcome with modern building blocks. Instead of an XML assertion, the identity provider issues an ID token, which is a signed JWT describing the user.

{
  "iss": "https://idp.example.com",
  "sub": "user-8842",
  "email": "dev@example.com",
  "name": "A. Developer",
  "exp": 1735689600
}

The service provider validates the JWT signature and reads the claims. Because JWTs are compact and JSON based, OIDC works cleanly for single page apps and mobile clients where heavy XML handling would be awkward. This is why most new SSO integrations choose OIDC.

OIDC also standardizes discovery, so a client can fetch a well known configuration document from the identity provider and learn every endpoint and signing key automatically. This makes integrating a new application far quicker than the manual certificate exchange that SAML often requires.
9. Sessions and Tokens in SSO
There are two layers of session in any SSO system, and confusing them causes bugs.

["The identity provider session proves the user has authenticated centrally. It is what makes the second and later logins seamless.","Each service provider session is the local session the application creates after it accepts the proof. It governs how long that one app stays logged in."]
items: The identity provider session proves the user has authenticated centrally. It is what makes the second and later logins seamless.
Each service provider session is the local session the application creates after it accepts the proof. It governs how long that one app stays logged in.

blocks.content: These can have different lifetimes. An application session might last an hour while the identity provider session lasts all day. When an application session expires, the user bounces back to the identity provider, which may silently re issue proof if its own session is still valid.
Silent re authentication

This bounce is usually invisible. The application redirects to the identity provider, the identity provider sees its own valid session and immediately redirects back with fresh proof, and the user notices nothing but a quick flicker. Only when the identity provider session has also expired does the user see a login screen again.
10. Single Logout
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785277780948-727200.png
Logging in once is convenient, but it raises a hard question: what should logging out do. If a user signs out of one application, should they be signed out of all of them.

["Local logout ends only the current application session. The user is still signed in elsewhere.","Single Logout tells the identity provider to end the central session and notify every application to end theirs too."]
items: Local logout ends only the current application session. The user is still signed in elsewhere.
Single Logout tells the identity provider to end the central session and notify every application to end theirs too.

blocks.content: Single Logout is genuinely harder to implement reliably, because the identity provider must reach every application that has an active session, and any one of them can fail to respond. Many systems settle for ending the identity provider session and letting application sessions expire naturally.
Front channel and back channel logout
blocks.text: Front channel and back channel logout

blocks.content: There are two ways to notify applications. Front channel logout loads a logout URL for each application in the browser, which is simple but fails silently if a tab is closed. Back channel logout has the identity provider call each application server directly, which is more reliable but requires every application to expose and secure a logout endpoint. Neither is trivial to make fully dependable.

blocks.title: A common interview trap
blocks.content: Single Logout is not automatic. It requires the identity provider to actively notify each service provider, and network failures make full, instant logout across all apps difficult to guarantee.
11. SSO vs Related Approaches
SSO is often confused with a few similar sounding ideas. Drawing the lines shows depth.

{"headers":["Approach","What it really is"],"rows":[["Single Sign-On","One trusted login unlocks many independent applications"],["Password Manager","Still separate logins; a tool just fills each password for you"],["Social Login","Using a public provider like Google as your identity provider"],["Same Sign-On","The same credentials copied into each app, but each still logs you in separately"]]}

A password manager does not remove the many separate logins; it only makes typing them easier. Social login is essentially SSO where the identity provider is a public consumer service. Same sign on shares credentials but not sessions, so it is not true SSO.
12. Benefits and Tradeoffs

{"headers":["Benefits","Tradeoffs"],"rows":[["One login for many apps, a smooth user experience","The identity provider becomes a single point of failure; if it is down, nobody logs in"],["Central place to enforce strong auth and multi factor","It is a high value target, so its compromise is severe"],["Instant offboarding by disabling one account","Integration and correct configuration take real effort"],["Applications stop storing passwords, shrinking risk","Single Logout is hard to get fully right"]]}

The central tradeoff is concentration. SSO concentrates convenience and control, but it also concentrates risk and availability requirements onto the identity provider, which must be highly available and very well secured.

This is why mature SSO deployments treat the identity provider as tier zero infrastructure. It is given redundancy across regions, aggressive monitoring, and strict change control, because its downtime blocks every employee from every tool at once.
13. Common Security Risks
Because SSO centralizes identity, its failure modes are high impact and worth naming.

["If the identity provider is compromised, every connected application is exposed at once.","A weak identity provider session, such as one that never expires, extends the blast radius of a stolen device.","Misconfigured trust, such as accepting assertions from the wrong issuer, can let attackers forge identities.","Not validating signatures or token expiry at the service provider undermines the whole model."]
items: If the identity provider is compromised, every connected application is exposed at once.
A weak identity provider session, such as one that never expires, extends the blast radius of a stolen device.
Misconfigured trust, such as accepting assertions from the wrong issuer, can let attackers forge identities.
Not validating signatures or token expiry at the service provider undermines the whole model.

blocks.title: Defense in depth
blocks.content: Protect the identity provider with strong multi factor authentication, short sensible session lifetimes, and strict validation of issuer, audience, signature, and expiry at every service provider.
14. When to Use SSO
SSO is worth its complexity once you cross a certain scale of applications or users.

["An organization running several internal applications for the same set of employees.","A product suite where users expect one account across all features.","Any environment where fast, complete offboarding is a security or compliance requirement.","Consumer products that want to offer login through Google, Apple, or similar providers."]
items: An organization running several internal applications for the same set of employees.
A product suite where users expect one account across all features.
Any environment where fast, complete offboarding is a security or compliance requirement.
Consumer products that want to offer login through Google, Apple, or similar providers.

blocks.content: For a single standalone application with its own users, SSO adds overhead without much benefit. The value grows with the number of applications that share the same users.

A practical middle ground for smaller products is to adopt a hosted identity provider rather than building one. This gives you the login experience and central control of SSO without operating the most security sensitive piece yourself.
15. Interview Points and Common Questions
What is the difference between an IdP and an SP: the identity provider authenticates the user and issues proof; the service provider is the application that trusts that proof and grants access.
Why does the second app not ask me to log in: the identity provider already has an active session for you, so it issues fresh proof without prompting for credentials.
SAML or OIDC: SAML for established enterprise integrations that expect XML; OpenID Connect for modern web and mobile because it uses compact JSON and JWTs.
What is the biggest risk of SSO: the identity provider is a single point of failure and a high value target, so its availability and security are critical.
Is Single Logout automatic: no, the identity provider must actively notify every application, and doing so reliably across all of them is difficult.
16. Key Takeaways

The identity provider authenticates; service providers trust the proof it issues.
The seamless second login comes from an existing session at the identity provider.
SAML uses signed XML assertions; OpenID Connect uses signed JWT ID tokens on top of OAuth.
There are two session layers: one at the identity provider and one at each application.
